passage: Jeevan, seventeen months, was at the third-floor window of the flat when a cow ambled down the colony lane. His mouth fell open. He stood very still, one hand gripping the grille, eyes fixed on the huge brown shape. Rashmi, his mother, came up behind him and smiled. “Cow. Look, a gentle cow.” Just then a scooter horn blared below and Jeevan jerked, then peered up at his mother's calm face. His mouth slowly closed into a small, wobbly grin, and he pointed.

qa.q: What did Jeevan see from the window?
qa.a: A cow walking down the colony lane.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have felt when his mouth fell open, and what else could it be?
qa.a: It could be wonder at seeing something so big, as his fixed stare and pointing show. It could also have been the start of fear, since he gripped the grille and froze when the horn sounded.

qa.q: What made it easier for Jeevan to settle?
qa.a: Rashmi's calm smile and simple words gave him something to read. She could also stay beside him and keep naming what he sees.

qa.q: What might Rashmi be noticing about her son?
qa.a: She might see that he looks to her face when something surprising happens, and that her own calm helps him choose how to feel. 🙂

grounding: A toddler's open-mouthed stare at a new animal and a sudden noise could be wonder, startle or fear, and a caregiver's calm face helps.

passage:
“Kiran! Look at your face,” said Baljeet. “Mouth wide open. What do you see?”
“Big,” Kiran whispered, pointing at the garden.
“That's Nani's tortoise. He's slow.”
Kiran stepped back and grabbed her father's trouser leg. “Bite?”
“No biting. Watch, he's eating a leaf.” Baljeet crouched and smiled.
“Nani, is he friendly?” he called.
“Very,” said Nani from the veranda.
Kiran peeked round his knee, mouth still open. “Leaf,” she said, and let go of the trouser.

qa.q: Whose tortoise was in the garden?
qa.a: It was Nani's tortoise, and Nani called from the veranda.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when she asked “Bite?”
qa.a: She seemed a little afraid, shown by stepping back and gripping her father's trouser leg. Her open mouth and stare could also mean she was fascinated, so probably she felt both.

qa.q: How did Baljeet help Kiran decide what to feel?
qa.a: He stayed calm, smiled, explained the tortoise was eating a leaf, and checked with Nani. He might also let her watch from a distance until she is ready.

qa.q: If Baljeet had jumped back and looked alarmed, what might have changed for Kiran?
qa.a: She might have taken his alarm as proof the animal was dangerous and become more frightened, rather than curious.

grounding: A toddler's open-mouthed look at a new animal mixes wonder and possible fear, and the caregiver's calm face settles it.

passage: Farm-visit note, playgroup, Friday. On the walk past the cowshed, a cow mooed very loudly right beside us. Zubin stopped. His mouth fell wide open and he stood stiff, staring at the cow. I wasn't sure if he was amazed or about to be frightened, so I kept my face easy and smiled at him. "Big moo!" I said softly. He looked at my face, then back at the cow, and pointed and laughed. He wanted to go closer. Karthik, playgroup helper

qa.q: What made Zubin stop on the walk?
qa.a: A cow mooed very loudly right beside them.

qa.q: What might Zubin's open mouth and stiff stance have meant?
qa.a: It could have been wonder at the huge sound or the start of fear; once he looked at Karthik's calm face, he seemed delighted, pointing and laughing.

qa.q: What did Karthik's calm reaction do for Zubin?
qa.a: It gave Zubin a steady face to check, which helped him treat the moo as funny instead of scary.

qa.q: If Karthik had gasped or pulled Zubin away, what might have changed?
qa.a: Zubin might have read the moment as danger and started to cry instead of wanting to go closer.

grounding: A toddler's open-mouthed stare at a sudden animal noise, which a helper's calm face helps him read as wonder rather than fear.

passage:
The temple fair in their small town was just waking up when the dhol players struck the first beat. Sunaina, perched on her brother Pranav's hip, went completely still. Her mouth dropped open and her eyes locked on the drummers. Pranav felt her fingers dig into his shirt.
He didn't hurry away. He grinned, swayed a little to the rhythm and said, "Dhum dhum!" Sunaina looked up at him, then back at the drums. Her mouth stayed open, but now her legs began to kick in time.

qa.q: Who was carrying Sunaina at the fair?
qa.a: Her brother Pranav was carrying her on his hip.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's grip on Pranav's shirt suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: Her open mouth showed surprise, and the digging fingers hint that she was close to being scared; after seeing Pranav grin, her kicking legs suggest excitement took over.

qa.q: What small step helped Sunaina here?
qa.a: Pranav stayed relaxed, swayed to the beat and named the sound, giving her a calm face to copy.

qa.q: How might it feel for Pranav when Sunaina's legs start kicking in time?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and pleased, knowing his little sister was enjoying the drums rather than frightened. 😊

grounding: A toddler's open-mouthed stare at a sudden loud drum, turned toward wonder by an older sibling's calm, cheerful face.

passage: In the park near their Osaka flat, a whole flock of pigeons burst up from the path at once. Hiroshi's mouth fell open. His lower lip began to shake. Esther, his childminder, kept pushing the stroller slowly and said in an easy voice, "Birds flying. Up, up!" She pointed and smiled. Hiroshi turned to study her face. His lip went still. He watched the birds circle the trees, mouth still round, and whispered, "Up."

qa.q: What made Hiroshi's mouth fall open?
qa.a: A whole flock of pigeons burst up from the path at once.

qa.q: What was Hiroshi likely feeling when his lip began to shake, and how did it change?
qa.a: He was probably startled and close to fear; after checking Esther's calm face, he seemed curious and full of wonder, whispering "Up."

qa.q: What would you advise a carer when a toddler looks startled like this?
qa.a: Keep your own voice and face calm, name what is happening and let the child look at you, as Esther did.

qa.q: If Esther had jumped too, how might Hiroshi have reacted?
qa.a: He would likely have read her fright as a sign of danger and started crying.

grounding: A toddler's open-mouthed startle at a sudden sight, which a carer's calm face helps turn into wonder.

passage:
I'm Thomas from the ground floor. Yesterday a goat wandered into our colony car park, and little Avni from upstairs was out with her father.
She stopped dead. Mouth wide open, eyes on the goat, not a sound. I honestly couldn't tell if she was about to laugh or scream.
Then she turned and looked up at her father. He smiled, easy, and said, “Goat! Baa!”
Avni looked back at the goat, pointed, and giggled. She wanted to follow it all the way to the gate.

qa.q: Where did the goat wander in?
qa.a: It wandered into the colony car park.

qa.q: What was Avni likely feeling with her mouth wide open, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: She was most likely surprised and full of wonder at a new animal, though it could have been the start of fear; she checked her father's face to decide.

qa.q: How could a caregiver help a toddler in a moment like this?
qa.a: Stay calm, smile and name the thing, as Avni's father did, so the child can read the adult's face and feel safe.

qa.q: How does Thomas see Avni's open-mouthed stare?
qa.a: Thomas couldn't tell whether she would laugh or scream until she looked at her father and then giggled.

grounding: It shows a toddler staring open-mouthed at a new animal, which could be wonder or fear, and a caregiver's calm face helping her decide.
